shots.src: GPS.gov · constellation in medium Earth orbit, ~20,200 km
shots.narration: Right now, about thirty satellites are flying twenty thousand kilometers above you. {p} Every one of them carries an atomic clock. {p} Your phone listens to those clocks to work out where you are. {pp} But there's a problem. Those clocks run fast.

shots.src: Uncorrected relativistic clock offset × speed of light
shots.title: GPS error if nobody fixed the clocks
shots.narration: Only by about thirty-eight millionths of a second a day. {p} Sounds like nothing. {p} But if nobody corrected it, GPS would drift by about eleven kilometers, every single day. {pp} The fix comes from Albert Einstein, and from two ideas most people think only matter near black holes. {p} It might be the most useful thing relativity has ever done. {p} Let's see how a few billionths of a second decide whether your map puts you on the right street.

shots.src: GPS signal: satellite ID + exact send time; range = travel time × speed of light
shots.narration: First, how GPS actually works. {p} Each satellite constantly broadcasts a simple message: who it is, and exactly what time it sent the signal. {p} Your phone notes when the signal arrives. {p} The difference is how long the signal traveled. {p} And since radio waves move at the speed of light, travel time tells you distance.

shots.title: light, per nanosecond
shots.narration: The catch is how fast light is. {p} In one billionth of a second, a nanosecond, light travels about thirty centimeters. {p} So if your clock is off by just one millionth of a second, your position is off by about three hundred meters. {p} GPS is really a timing system that happens to tell you where you are.

shots.src: Trilateration: 3 ranges fix a point; the 4th satellite solves the receiver clock error
shots.narration: With the distance to three satellites, your phone can pin down a single point. {p} But your phone has a cheap quartz clock, nowhere near an atomic one. {p} So it uses a fourth satellite to solve for the time as well. {p} Four satellites, four unknowns: where you are, in three dimensions, and what time it really is. {p} Usually your phone can see more than four, and uses the extras to sharpen the fix.

shots.title: The satellites
shots.narration: So everything depends on the satellite clocks being perfect. {p} They're atomic clocks, cesium and rubidium, accurate to a few billionths of a second. {p} They orbit about twenty thousand kilometers up, going around the Earth twice a day, at almost fourteen thousand kilometers an hour. {p} And that's exactly where Einstein comes in. Twice.

shots.title: special relativity: speed slows time
shots.src: Δt ≈ v²/2c² per second · v ≈ 3.87 km/s
shots.narration: Effect number one: speed. {p} Einstein's special relativity says a moving clock ticks slower than one standing still. {p} At fourteen thousand kilometers an hour, the satellite clocks lose about seven millionths of a second every day, compared with clocks on the ground.

lines.note: µs lost per day (moving clock ticks slower)

shots.title: general relativity: gravity slows time
shots.src: Δt ≈ GM(1/R⊕ − 1/r)/c² per second · r ≈ 26,560 km
shots.narration: Effect number two: gravity. {p} Einstein's general relativity says clocks run slower deeper in a gravity well. {p} We're down here, deep in Earth's gravity. The satellites are far above it, where gravity is weaker. {p} So from our point of view, their clocks run faster, by about forty-five millionths of a second a day.

lines.note: µs gained per day (weaker gravity → faster clock)

shots.title: Satellite clock vs ground clock, per day
shots.narration: Put them together. {p} Minus seven for speed, plus forty-five for gravity. {pp} The satellite clocks gain about thirty-eight millionths of a second every day. {p} The two effects fight each other, and gravity wins.

shots.src: Hafele & Keating, Science 177 (1972) · flights of October 1971
shots.title: 1971: four atomic clocks on airliners
shots.narration: If that sounds too weird to be real, it was tested with plane tickets. {p} In 1971, two physicists, Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating, flew four atomic clocks around the world on ordinary passenger jets, then compared them with clocks left on the ground. {p} Flying east, the clocks lost about fifty-nine billionths of a second. {p} Flying west, they gained about two hundred seventy-three. {pp} Within the error bars of what Einstein's theories predicted.

shots.title: 38 µs, in distance
shots.narration: Now turn that into distance. {p} Thirty-eight millionths of a second, times the speed of light, is about eleven thousand four hundred meters. {p} Eleven kilometers. {pp} After one day. {p} And the error doesn't reset. It keeps piling up: twenty-three kilometers after two days, about eighty after a week.

lines.note: km after 1 day, 2 days, a week

shots.narration: Your map wouldn't put you on the wrong street. {p} Within a week, it would put you in the wrong city. {p} Planes, ships, farm tractors, phone networks and banks, which all use GPS time, {pp} would slowly drift out of sync with reality.

items.text: Networks and banks use GPS time too

shots.src: 3GPP TDD phase sync (±1.5 µs) · EU MiFID II RTS 25 (HFT timestamps ≤100 µs from UTC)
shots.title: Who else runs on GPS time
shots.narration: And it's not just maps. {p} Many cell towers use GPS time to stay in sync with each other, to within about one and a half millionths of a second. {p} In Europe, high-frequency traders must time-stamp their trades to within a tenth of a millisecond of official time, and many firms get that time from satellites. {pp} A clock drifting thirty-eight microseconds a day would knock those cell towers out of sync in about an hour, and the traders within three days.

items.text: cell networks: in sync to ~1.5 µs
EU high-frequency trading: ≤100 µs from UTC
38 µs/DAY: TOWERS OUT OF SYNC IN ~1 HOUR

shots.title: the factory setting
shots.src: Misra, GPS World (2023) · Bahder, arXiv gr-qc/0306076
shots.narration: So how do you fix a clock that runs fast in space? {p} You make it run slow on the ground. {p} GPS clocks are built to tick at ten point two three megahertz. {p} But before launch, they're set to ten point two two nine nine nine nine nine nine nine five four three. {p} On the ground, that's slightly slow. In orbit, relativity speeds it up to exactly right. {p} And ground stations still watch every satellite clock, and upload small corrections to each one, usually at least once a day.

shots.src: Ashby, 'General relativity in the Global Positioning System' (APS Matters of Gravity, 1997)
shots.title: NTS-2, June 1977
shots.narration: Not everyone believed it at first. And the skeptics weren't crazy: nobody had ever put a cesium clock in orbit before. {p} In June 1977, the first test satellite with a cesium clock, NTS-2, went up with a switch on board, so the correction could be turned on later. {p} For twenty days, engineers let the clock run uncorrected. {p} It ran fast by four hundred forty-two parts in a trillion. {p} Einstein predicted four hundred forty-six. {pp} Less than one percent off. Then they flipped the switch.

items.text: 23 Jun 1977 · NTS-2: first cesium clock in orbit

shots.title: Corrections still running today
shots.narration: And that's not the only correction. {p} GPS orbits aren't perfect circles, so each clock speeds up and slows down a little as its height changes. Your receiver corrects for that too. {p} The Earth also rotates while the signal is in flight, adding another tiny shift. {p} Every position fix quietly accounts for all of it. {p} And it's not just GPS. Europe's Galileo, Russia's GLONASS and China's BeiDou all have to make the same relativity corrections.

items.text: slightly oval orbits: clock rate wobbles
Earth rotates during the signal's trip

shots.src: Penn State GEOG 862 · GPS.gov (Selective Availability, May 2000)
shots.title: Wrong on purpose, part two
shots.narration: And here's a twist. For years, GPS was also made wrong on purpose, for a different reason. {p} Until 2000, the US military deliberately jittered the satellite clocks for civilian users, a feature called Selective Availability. {p} Your position could be off by about a hundred meters. {p} On May second, 2000, it was switched off, and civilian GPS got about ten times more accurate overnight.

So, the next time your phone finds you on a map, remember what's happening. {p} Clocks in orbit, running fast because gravity is weaker up there, and slow because they're moving, {p} set wrong on purpose, so they'd be right in space. {pp} Relativity isn't just for black holes. {p} It's in your pocket.

yt.title: GPS Only Works Because of Einstein
yt.description:
GPS satellite clocks run fast by about 38 microseconds a day. Uncorrected, your position would drift about 11 km every day. How GPS turns time into distance, the two relativity effects that fight each other in orbit, the clock that's set wrong on purpose, and the 1977 satellite that proved Einstein right.

Sources: GPS.gov; N. Ashby, 'General relativity in the Global Positioning System' (APS, 1997) and Living Reviews in Relativity (2003); P. Misra, 'Inside the box: GPS and relativity', GPS World (2023); T. Bahder, arXiv gr-qc/0306076.
